items.title: Artificial intelligence algorithms for complex industrial optimization
items.abstract: We organize the research needs around three connected challenges: AI-assisted problem formulation and structural representation; scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains; and closed-loop adaptation in dynamic, uncertain, and multi-objective environments. Two requirements cut across all three challenges: structure-aware integration of optimization, learning, and simulation; and operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability. In the latter, information, tasks, and decision authority are allocated among domain experts, operators, AI assistants and agents, optimizers, and simulators according to risk and context (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Industrial optimization begins before a solver is selected. Relevant information is distributed across data systems, engineering documents, regulations, and expert practice. These sources differ in timing, vocabulary, and reliability. Model formulation requires identification of the decisions, objectives, constraints, uncertainties, and couplings that define the operational problem. Translating an agreed description into equations is only one part of that task.Methods for constraint acquisition can infer candidate rules from examples and expert queries (Bessiere et al., 2017), while decision-focused approaches can optimize predictive models for downstream decision quality (Donti et al., 2017;Wilder et al., 2019). Rules inferred from data or text remain provisional until they are checked against actual operations. Each candidate rule requires verification of its provenance, scope, conflicts with other rules, and operational consequences before it enters a decision model. Human skills, decision rights, and handoff responsibilities may themselves be part of the modeled structure, particularly when tasks can move between people and automated components (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents can mediate between informal descriptions and formal optimization models. They can propose formulations, generate solver code, and assign modeling or verification tasks to specialized components (Zhang et al., 2024a;Xiao et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2026). Recent work that combines LLM-based extraction with reusable modeling graphs and expert-defined templates illustrates a more controlled division of responsibility (Li et al., 2026). These outputs remain candidate models. Solver execution can expose coding errors or infeasibility, but it cannot establish semantic completeness or show that an omitted business rule is inconsequential.A traceable modeling loop records how constraints are acquired and classified, who validates them, how uncertainty and problem structure are represented, and when operational change triggers model revision. If the resulting problem is infeasible, the algorithm needs to identify the conflicting assumptions and return either an interpretable relaxation or a safe recovery action. Evaluation then turns on downstream decision performance under missing or changing information; fluent model generation alone is insufficient.The computational burden of large industrial optimization problems arises from both problem size and coordination across resources, organizations, and time scales. Machines, workforce capabilities, energy supply, inventory, and transport capacity are coupled through shared constraints, but their influence on system performance is unequal and state dependent. A disruption can shift the bottleneck from equipment to technicians, spare parts, storage, or transport. Algorithms need representations and sensitivity measures that identify the binding couplings and detect when those relationships change.In distributed scheduling, job-to-factory assignment and within-factory sequencing are interdependent (Naderi and Ruiz, 2010). Across a supply chain, procurement, production, inventory, and delivery decisions are made over different planning horizons. Solving these stages separately can shift costs, delays, or emissions downstream; even under restricted assumptions, integrated production-inventory-delivery models are computationally demanding (Gen et al., 2008;Li et al., 2017). Coordination also involves organizations, human planners, and AI agents that hold different information and decision rights. Recent supply-chain research on agentic AI accordingly treats human-agent roles and organizational constraints as design choices rather than assuming full autonomy (Trifone et al., 2026).Decomposition and mathematical programming can exploit sparsity and explicit constraint structure, while evolutionary algorithms and large-neighborhood search can explore difficult discrete and nonconvex search spaces (Yu and Gen, 2010;Pisinger and Ropke, 2010). A central design question is how to balance global exploration with local improvement. Global moves reallocate orders, capacity, and supply-chain flows; local moves refine sequences, routes, and maintenance schedules. Learned components may select neighborhoods, warm starts, decompositions, or algorithm configurations. Their value depends on preserving global consistency while reducing end-to-end decision time and resource use. A learned policy may improve one subproblem yet render another infeasible when cross-stage constraints are omitted, represented too coarsely, or invalidated by a disruption. Learned guidance also needs to recognize when a fixed decomposition is no longer valid.Multiple objectives introduce an additional tension between computational efficiency and decision effectiveness. Efficiency concerns whether an algorithm returns an answer before the decision deadline. Effectiveness covers feasibility, solution-set quality and diversity, and alignment with decision-maker preferences (Deb et al., 2002;Zhang et al., 2024b). Automated program search can generate heuristics and search rules, including variants for multi-objective optimization (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2025). Their performance remains uncertain when the evaluation function overlooks cross-stage couplings. Evaluation should establish whether local gains persist once supply-chain interactions are accounted for and whether a globally consistent plan can be produced on time.Demand, resource availability, prices, and customer priorities change over different time scales. Parameter uncertainty, observed disruptions, distribution shift, and structural change each call for a different response. Repeatedly running a static optimizer after every event does not by itself create a closed-loop strategy.A closed-loop algorithm links state estimation and prediction to model revision, optimization, execution, and feedback. Robust planning and reactive rescheduling play complementary roles and can be coordinated through rolling-horizon optimization, online learning, dynamic optimization, and calibrated simulation. Full regeneration may improve the objective value but increase schedule nervousness; local repair preserves stability but can lock in a poor global allocation (Vieira et al., 2003;Blackburn et al., 1986). Reinforcement learning can represent delayed consequences, but exploration in industrial systems must respect constraints during training and deployment. A high expected return does not establish acceptable tail risk or recoverability (García and Fernández, 2015;Wachi et al., 2024). Recent dynamic-scheduling work shows how a formal supervisor can restrict reinforcement learning to a safe, non-blocking operating space and support rapid recovery after disruptions (Wang et al., 2026).Digital twins are useful for stress testing only if their models remain valid under the disruptions that drive decisions (Tao et al., 2019). Emerging architectures connect digital twins, multiple agents, online multi-objective optimization, and human-robot collaboration (Huang et al., 2026). These combinations strengthen the case for a closed loop, but they also increase the number of interfaces whose state, latency, and failure modes need monitoring.Priorities assigned to cost, service, sustainability, resilience, and workload may also change during a disruption. Adaptation therefore requires more than repeated static Pareto optimization. The algorithm needs to choose among continuing or repairing the current plan, re-optimizing, updating the model, and escalating the decision to a human decision-maker. Task and decision authority may also need to shift as risk, AI confidence, human workload, and time pressure change. Evaluation needs to report feasibility under distributional and structural shifts, tail-risk and recovery metrics, and operational gains net of excessive plan changes.Hybrid algorithmic architectures are justified only when their components perform distinct, necessary functions, their interfaces can be validated, and the integrated method outperforms a strong but simpler baseline (Fan et al., 2026;Wiberg et al., 2026). Learning can estimate uncertain states or surrogate models and select search controls when equivalent information is unavailable within the operational deadline. Mathematical and constraint programming can enforce explicit feasibility logic and provide bounds. Evolutionary algorithms are useful for discrete, nonconvex, black-box, or preference-sensitive search, whereas simulation represents behavior that is difficult to express analytically.The interfaces between components deserve equal scrutiny because they govern information exchange, uncertainty propagation, and failure detection. A learned initialization may accelerate a solver yet fail under distribution shift. Likewise, a high-fidelity simulation may consume the computation needed for adequate stress testing. Ablation studies need to test both individual contributions and failures at component interfaces under the same operational budget.A learning-based or generative component may propose a formulation or heuristic; a solver, simulator, or explicit checker can then test it. The inclusion of every added component should be justified by a verifiable improvement in decision quality. This division of responsibility is especially important for LLM-based agents, whose ability to orchestrate tools does not remove the need for formal checks and controlled access to operational systems.Operational reliability depends on how an algorithm interacts with enterprise data flows, shop-floor execution systems, and human decision-makers. Stale state information, interface mismatches, human overrides, and execution deviations can all change the optimization problem. Monitoring, rollback, reoptimization, escalation, and revalidation are consequently part of the algorithm lifecycle.The appropriate unit of analysis is the hybrid decision team rather than the AI component in isolation.Its performance depends on how information, tasks, and authority are distributed among operators, managers, AI agents, optimization solvers, and organizational units. Human participants can contribute tacit knowledge and handle exceptions, but poor handoffs or unclear authority can delay responses and obscure accountability. Experimental evidence from AI-assisted production indicates that team organization affects failure recovery through the frequency and quality of communication (Krzywdzinski et al., 2026). Semantic models for dynamic work sharing offer one way to represent changing human and artificial roles, although their contribution must ultimately be tested through team and system outcomes (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Accordingly, evaluation should include communication quality, handoff latency, calibrated reliance, intervention workload, recovery performance, and operational outcomes alongside conventional algorithmic metrics. Explanations need separate scrutiny: in a job-shop scheduling experiment, brief AI rationales increased behavioral reliance without necessarily improving understanding (Saßmannshausen et al., 2026). Trust, reliance, and decision correctness are distinct measures.Claims of improvement require comparison against competitive optimization, learning, and engineering baselines under matched end-to-end resource budgets. Those budgets include data preparation, model development, computation, simulation, and human effort. Experiments need to vary coupling strength, constraint tightness, disruption severity, distribution shift, and decision deadlines rather than instance size alone. Studies should also report prediction quality, optimization quality, and operational value separately. Optimization quality includes feasibility, optimality gap, regret, and Pareto-front approximation quality; operational value includes plan stability, service performance, recovery time, and integration effort.Fluent formulations and executable code do not establish correctness. Grounded in solver functions, LLM interfaces can nevertheless support infeasibility diagnosis, sensitivity analysis, and what-if or why-not queries (Chen et al., 2025). High-consequence decisions still require traceable constraints, validated alternatives, controlled system access, and explicit human authority over rollback and escalation.The three challenges span problem formulation and structural representation, scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains, and closed-loop adaptation. Success depends on a faithful operational model, coordination of coupled decisions within the available time, and revision of those decisions without sacrificing feasibility or stability. Structure-aware integration determines whether the algorithmic components work together; operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability determine whether gains at one stage translate into system-level performance.Prediction accuracy, average reward, isolated benchmark gains, and the addition of another AI component provide incomplete evidence of progress. The stronger standard is better decision quality under realistic constraints, coupling, and change, together with communication and authority arrangements that support timely intervention and recovery. Ultimately, an industrial AI algorithm needs to solve the right problem within the decision deadline and continue to produce feasible, stable, and controllable decisions as operating conditions change.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and AI-Related Digital Systems in Tourism Companies: Knowledge, Adoption, Perceived Effects, and Stakeholder Comparisons
items.abstract: This study examines knowledge, broad reported use, and the perceived effects of artificial intelligence (AI) and related digital systems through an exploratory secondary analysis of 323 company-survey responses. The numerical source is a previously unused company-side aggregate results report from the research programme associated with an earlier published tourist study, with waves labelled 2024 (n = 162) and 2026 (n = 161). Biosphere Portugal’s practice-informed project documentation provides complementary sustainability context. The contribution is an analysis and interpretation of existing aggregate evidence, not a new primary survey or longitudinal panel. Company-level microdata were not available for this analysis. Acceptance and organisational-readiness perspectives guide four research questions. The broad survey indicator records 190 affirmative responses (58.8%) but does not establish verified AI adoption. Conflicting pooled and wave-specific technology counts are preserved as unresolved source discrepancies rather than treated as corrected ground truth. Descriptive group contrasts are reported without inferential significance claims because item-specific valid-case denominators, missing-response coding and cross-wave independence cannot be verified from the archived aggregate materials. The analysis is therefore confined to broad reported-use status and function labels, not AI-specific user effects. Published tourist findings are compared thematically rather than pooled. The implications concern the measurement discipline, context-dependent capability, governance, and sustainability assessment; perceived efficiency benefits are not treated as measured net sustainability gains.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Destiny: Beyond War and Solvency
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is no longer merely a technological innovation; it is a transformative force reshaping economic systems, institutional responsibilities, social relations, and the collective understanding of progress. This article interprets AI as an expression of humanity’s enduring ambition to reproduce aspects of itself in an artificial entity capable of imitating language, reasoning, and behavior without necessarily possessing consciousness. Starting from the debate on accelerating technological change and the disputed prospect of a technological singularity, it distinguishes measurable advances from speculative scenarios and examines the conceptual distance between specialized AI, artificial general intelligence, and superintelligence. Particular attention is devoted to artificial consciousness: sophisticated responses and autonomous analysis may simulate human abilities, but they do not yet demonstrate the existence of subjective experience. This uncertainty calls for scientific caution, transparent criteria, and an interdisciplinary debate involving technical, philosophical, ethical, legal, and political perspectives. The analysis then connects the governance of AI with broader human challenges. Technological development should not be directed solely toward greater productive power, but toward overcoming war, reducing inequalities created by economic exclusion, improving care and scientific research, strengthening security, and widening access to the goods essential to life. In this perspective, robots and intelligent systems may assist families, older people, hospitals, universities, and research centers, provided that their deployment remains subject to human responsibility and democratic control. The renewed space race offers a parallel case: international cooperation, private enterprise, and large-scale finance now converge in projects ranging from orbital infrastructure to the prospect of human settlements beyond Earth. The ambitions surrounding SpaceX and other private actors therefore reveal how technological visions, collective risks, and market valuations have become increasingly intertwined. Rather than presenting progress as either automatic salvation or inevitable catastrophe, the article argues for a new exodus: a human-centered path beyond violence, exclusion, and, eventually, the limits of Earth. Such a path requires shared international rules capable of preventing unrestrained competition from rewarding less responsible actors and of ensuring that innovation remains accountable to human dignity, peace, inclusion, and future generations.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Resources Management in Cameroon’s Public Sector
items.abstract: The use of AI in African public human resource management (HRM) is still a largely unexplored area. This sequential mixed-methods study takes a closer look at how AI is accepted within Cameroon’s Ministry of Public Works (MINTP), drawing on 32 interviews analyzed with NVivo and 653 questionnaires processed through structural equation modeling (SEM). On the theoretical side, this paper breaks new ground by blending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Resource-Based View (RBV) with the idea of digital discretion. It introduces the fresh concept of ‘reserve discretion,’ which refers to the right of human appeal acting as a sort of a posteriori human veto. The qualitative results show that people are generally okay with AI handling routine, standardized tasks but are much less comfortable when it comes to decisions requiring human judgment. Meanwhile, the structural equation analysis reveals that psychological factors like concerns over traceability and loss of control pose much bigger obstacles to AI adoption than technical infrastructure issues. Ultimately, having a clearly defined right to human appeal plays a major role in encouraging users to adopt AI, supporting a model of hybrid public governance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights in the Context of Globalization. Challenges and European Regulations in Romania
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in public administration, education and other sensitive areas raises essential questions about fairness, transparency and the protection of fundamental rights. The article addresses a central question: how can AI be regulated in a way that respects human dignity and protects fundamental rights? Starting from the European framework, with a focus on the AI Act and its human-centric approach to AI governance, the article provides a critical analysis of how these requirements are reflected in national realities. The Romanian case study highlights the gap between regulatory ambitions and concrete implementation: from digital justice and public administration to the education system where algorithms are present without a real public debate. Issues including the need for ethical audit mechanisms, the scope of citizen involvement and systemic risks for vulnerable groups are discussed from an interdisciplinary and applied perspective. The article proposes several solutions to strengthen the democratic framework of AI: establishing real forms of public participation, developing tailored control and monitoring tools, and recognizing the role of universities in promoting an ethical culture of digitalization. Through its critical but constructive tone, the article not only assesses existing regulations, but also provides a direction for the future – one in which technology serves people rather than replacing human judgment. Keywords: artificial intelligence; globalization; AI Act; algorithmic discrimination; data protection

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Applications Using Indian Electronic Health Records
items.abstract: Advanced analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) methods have been increasingly utilized with electronic health records (EHRs) to assist patient care in health systems around the world. EHR adaptation is growing in India. Several institutions have been performing extensive evaluations of AI methods to predict and analyze health outcomes utilizing routinely collected EHR data. Currently, limited studies have reviewed and synthesized the application of AI and machine learning (ML) methods to Indian EHR data. The objective of this narrative review study was to summarize the articles that use AI/ML methods to analyze Indian EHR data, defining the present state of EHR-based modelling to support patient care. A search for articles was conducted in PubMed to identify peer-reviewed articles published between January 1, 2015, and December 1, 2025, that utilized EHR data created in India and used AI/ML techniques to conduct analytical or predictive analyses. Two independent reviewers screened and reviewed the identified studies. Data extraction included source of data, clinical domain, model development methods, and performance measures and results. Extracted data were summarized in a narrative form. Out of the included studies, most were based on large ophthalmology health systems and tertiary cardiology hospitals, with one focused on COVID-19 outcomes. Additionally, most utilized some type of statistical, ML, or AI modelling, such as SARIMA forecasting, multivariate regression, rule-based natural language processing, and deep learning, whereas a few only focused on descriptive analyses of EHR big data. Results show strong performance of the AI/ML models in answering a variety of clinical questions including cardiovascular risk prediction, outpatient forecasting, and text extraction. In summary, the studies show potential in future applications of AI/ML models in revolutionizing Indian patient care utilizing Indian EHR data.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Authority of Student Knowledge: The Perspective of the Purification of Islamic Teachings by Muhammad Abduh
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has brought significant changes to the way students acquire, validate, and understand knowledge, particularly in Islamic studies. The growing dependence on AI has generated epistemological issues related to authority of knowledge, as algorithm based digital information is often perceived as faster and more practical than consulting authentic Islamic sources. This study aims to describe how the use of AI affects students' knowledge authority within the framework of the purification of Islamic teachings as articulated by Muhammad Abduh. Employing a phenomenological method, the research involved ten students from various faculties at an Islamic higher education institution. Data were collected through observation, in depth interviews, and documentation, then analyzed through data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing. The findings reveal that while students utilize AI to support academic activities, most of them are not yet able to assess the validity of AI generated information based on the principles of revelation and reason. A phenomenon of "digital taqlid" emerges, in which information is accepted without verification. However, some students demonstrate critical use of AI and balance it with Islamic values, aligning with Abduh's purification framework that emphasizes rationality, ijtihad, and adherence to revelation. This study concludes that AI can be a beneficial tool when used selectively, critically, and grounded in the authoritative epistemology of Islam.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE: THE IMPACT OF GENERATIVE MODELS ON WRITTEN DISCOURSE, STYLE, AND LINGUISTIC COMPETENCE
items.abstract: This article examines the multifaceted impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on contemporary English written communication, with particular attention to generative models such as ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs). The analysis centers on written discourse, addressing stylistic formation, textual categories, genre conventions, and the redefinition of linguistic competence within digital contexts. Drawing on discourse analysis, stylistics, and sociolinguistics, the research demonstrates that AI technologies, functioning as both medium and mode of communication, are transforming textual conventions, challenging traditional notions of authorship, and blurring the distinction between human and machine discourse. The central argument asserts that AI operates not only as an autonomous agent in linguistic evolution – generating texts through specific algorithms – but also as a crucial driver of linguistic standardization. This process produces texts lacking human nuance, fosters stylistic and genre hybridization, and contributes to the emergence of a homogenized global form of English. Ultimately, LLMs signify a shift from individual to distributed cognition and from socially determined genre conventions to probabilistic constructions shaped by user input and computational recombination. The study concludes that heightened critical awareness of these developments is vital for preserving linguistic diversity and promoting interpretive literacy in an era increasingly shaped by algorithmic text production.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being touted as a catchall, ‘general-purpose technology' which can transform economic growth. AI, or ‘artificial intelligence ', is emerging as a ‘catch-all' or ‘general-purpose technology' with the capacity to drive economic growth. The effects on productivity, jobs, innovation, inequality, and sustainability have been debated. The objective of this review is to bring together the peer-reviewed and working paper literature relating to the subject during the period 2020– 2025. Experimental and firm-level studies indicate significant task-level productivity improvements, particularly for less experienced workers. In macroeconomics, estimates of aggregate gains do not exceed. As for employment, so far it is not mass displacement; rather, it is task reallocation, which, as is well known, occurs with automation and leads to wage polarisation. AI is creating innovations in science and biomedicine like protein structure prediction and drug discovery, but few companies and countries can develop AI. AI can help achieve climate and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), but it also has significant energy, carbon, and water impacts. We believe AI-powered growth is sustainable and inclusive only if complemented by appropriate investments in skills, governance, auditing, open infrastructure, and energy-efficient computing. We recommend a policy framework and research priorities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Reorientation of the Murabbi Role: Shifting from Knowledge Transmission to Spiritual Guidance
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical paradigms, particularly in knowledge delivery. In Islamic education, this technological shift poses a critical challenge to the role of the Murabbi (educator), risking a reduction of teaching to mere cognitive information transfer. This study aims to analyze the reorientation of the Murabbi role in the AI era, arguing for a paradigm shift from knowledge transmission to spiritual guidance. Employing a qualitative approach through library research and conceptual analysis, this study examines Islamic educational philosophy, particularly the concepts of Tarbiyah, Ta’dib, and the spiritual dimensions of teaching. The findings reveal that while AI can efficiently automate knowledge transmission and cognitive assessments, it is inherently incapable of fostering adab (moral disposition), providing uswah (exemplary character), and facilitating tazkiyatun nafs (purification of the soul). Consequently, the Murabbi must transition from being a primary source of information to a spiritual mentor and moral facilitator. This reorientation ensures that Islamic education preserves its transcendent goals amidst technological automation, offering a distinct pedagogical framework that integrates digital efficiency with the irreplaceable spiritual human connection.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Sports Refereeing: A Systematic Review and Methodological Comparison
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly being used in sports refereeing to support decision-making, object and event tracking, and player- or team-related analysis. This systematic review aimed to examine the application areas of AI technol-ogies in sports refereeing across different sports, identify the analytical methods em-ployed, and compare their methodological performance based on reported accuracy rates. The literature search and study selection process were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, EBSCO, and Google Scholar databases were searched using the string “((Artificial Intelligence) OR (machine learning) OR (deep learning)) AND Sport AND referee”. A total of 404 records were initially identified; after duplicate removal, 374 studies remained. Following title and abstract screening, 45 articles were assessed in full text, and 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. The findings showed that AI applications were predominantly implemented in football. The primary application areas were Referee Decision Support Systems (7 stud-ies), Object and Event Tracking (5 studies), and Player and Team Analysis (2 studies). The most frequently used methods included CNN, LSTM, and YOLO-based deep learning models. Image-processing-based models, particularly YOLO-based approaches, gener-ally demonstrated higher accuracy compared to sensor-based systems. Overall, AI has potential to enhance the accuracy of refereeing decisions and operational efficiency; however, performance limitations, data quality issues, and ethical concerns remain sig-nificant challenges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Distinguishing Glaucoma From Its Mimickers: A Narrative Review of Diagnostic Pitfalls, Validation Gaps, and Clinical Translation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly in glaucoma, but many models remain optimized for case‐control detection rather than the clinically harder task of distinguishing glaucoma from its mimickers. This narrative review primarily examined literature published from January 2018 to March 2026 on glaucoma AI, difficult comparator groups, external validation, uncertainty, and reporting quality. High myopia, physiologic cupping, congenital disc anomalies, compressive optic neuropathy, and non‐arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy remain major sources of diagnostic ambiguity. Recent studies show that machine learning can differentiate some of these entities, particularly on optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), yet such comparator‐rich designs remain uncommon. Landmark detection models still lose performance under dataset shift, and recent reviews document persistent deficiencies in transparency and early clinical reporting. The most clinically useful direction for glaucoma AI is therefore not detection alone, but mimicker‐aware validation, clinically grounded reference standards, uncertainty‐aware outputs, and multimodal decision support.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for extracellular vesicle engineering and therapeutic design
items.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are promising platforms for next-generation drug delivery and regenerative therapeutics, yet biological heterogeneity, limited targeting specificity, variable cargo composition, and continued reliance on empirical optimization hinder clinical translation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to make EV engineering more predictive and data-driven. Building on prior work in AI-assisted EV delivery and emerging virtual-EV modeling, this review presents an evidence-aware, multiscale framework that integrates parental-cell programming, vesicle design, recipient-system modeling, and experimental feedback. At the source level, AI virtual cells (AIVCs) may help predict how perturbations to parental cells influence EV biogenesis and composition. At the vesicle level, AI-guided approaches may support cargo prioritization, surface engineering, and loading optimization. At the recipient level, digital twin models could help simulate EV uptake, intracellular trafficking, microenvironmental interactions, and downstream therapeutic responses. These components may ultimately be integrated with experimental validation into iterative design-test-refinement workflows. Importantly, this review distinguishes direct EV-specific evidence from technologies transferable from adjacent fields and concepts that remain prospective. By defining these evidence boundaries and linking them to key challenges in data quality, model interpretability, manufacturing, and validation, this framework provides a practical roadmap for advancing AI-enabled EV therapeutics from conceptual modeling to testable, translationally relevant engineering strategies.

items.abstract: Modern times require smart solutions for crime detection to enhance public security levels because crime detection remains a fundamental challenge. The AI models perform two functions: detecting suspicious activities and identifying weapons and faces, and recognising patterns of criminal behaviour. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Opportunities, Risks and Responsible Use
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in education to support tutoring, assessment, content generation, administrative work and personalized learning. This paper reviews major educational opportunities and risks associated with AI systems, especially generative AI. The discussion shows that AI can improve access to feedback, reduce repetitive teacher workload and provide adaptive learning support, but it can also introduce inaccurate information, bias, privacy concerns and overdependence on automated tools. Effective use therefore requires human oversight, transparent policies, digital literacy and careful protection of student data. The paper concludes that AI is most useful when it augments, rather than replaces, the professional judgment of teachers and the active participation of learners.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in English Language Teaching: An Assessment of Teacher Comfort, Usage, Readiness, and Perceptions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping educational landscapes, yet its integration in developing contexts remains uneven due to significant infrastructural disparities. This study assessed the comfort, frequency of use, perceived usefulness, and readiness of K–12 English language teachers in the Philippines regarding AI integration. Grounded in the TPACK and SAMR frameworks, the study used a quantitative comparative research design, surveying 688 public school teachers from a highly urbanized division (Biñan City) and a predominantly rural division (Nueva Ecija). The findings reveal a distinct "readiness gap": teachers show high internal self-efficacy and comfort but report insufficient institutional support. While respondents frequently use AI for text-based administrative tasks, usage for transformative listening and speaking activities remains rare, indicating a stagnation at the "Substitution" level of technology integration. Statistical analysis confirms a significant "digital native" effect, where younger, early-career teachers exhibit greater adaptability than their seasoned peers. Crucially, a profound digital divide was identified, with urban teachers reporting significantly higher frequency of AI use (M = 3.98 vs. 3.25, t = 14.31, p < .001, d = 1.09) and readiness for integration (M = 4.05 vs. 3.41, t = 13.56, p < .001, d = 1.03) than their rural counterparts. The study also uncovered a pedagogical paradox wherein teachers acknowledge AI's utility but fear it diminishes students' critical thinking skills. These results challenge the efficacy of uniform training mandates, suggesting that sustainable integration requires differentiated strategies that prioritize infrastructural enablement in rural areas while focusing on ethical, pedagogical governance in urban settings. This research contributes to the literature by quantifying the impact of locational privilege on AI adoption and advocating context-sensitive policies to prevent deepening educational inequities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Facial Palsy: A Narrative Review Across the Care Continuum
items.abstract: Introduction Facial paralysis produces substantial functional and psychosocial impairment which facial reanimation surgery seeks to mitigate by restoring facial movement and improving symmetry. However, despite technical advances in nerve- and muscle-based reconstruction, perioperative evaluation and outcome assessment remain largely subjective and variably reproducible. Artificial intelligence (AI) and computer vision have emerged as tools to provide objective, scalable assessment across the facial reanimation care pathway. Methods MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched extensively to identify studies evaluating AI applications relevant to facial reanimation surgery. Included studies were screened by three independent reviewers and mapped to stages of perioperative care using an evidence-mapping framework. Results Thirteen studies met inclusion criteria and were distributed across multiple stages of care. Evidence was most concentrated in diagnosis and severity assessment and in postoperative follow-up, where AI systems automated facial grading scales, quantified asymmetry, and extracted dynamic motion features from photographs and video. Several machine learning and deep learning models demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and strong correlations with clinician-assigned scores, often exceeding inter-rater reliability of traditional grading systems. Fewer studies addressed prognostic modeling, preoperative planning, or rehabilitation, though emerging applications included outcome prediction, three-dimensional symmetry analysis, and AI-assisted evaluation of spontaneous emotional expression after reanimation. Conclusion AI applications in facial paralysis care are most mature in assessment and outcome measurement, where they offer improved objectivity and reproducibility. However, broader clinical integration will require larger, diverse datasets, prospective validation, and alignment with ethical and regulatory standards to demonstrate meaningful patient centered benefit.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Vehicular Networks: A Comprehensive Review of Security Challenges and Defenses
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into vehicular networks has fundamentally transformed intelligent transportation systems, enabling autonomous driving, cooperative perception, and real-time traffic management. However, this convergence has simultaneously expanded the security attack surface, creating novel vulnerabilities that traditional cryptographic defenses alone cannot address. This comprehensive review examines the intersection of AI, vehicular networks, and security, providing a systematic analysis of emerging threats and defense mechanisms. We first establish the architectural foundations of modern vehicular networks, tracing the evolution from Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs) to the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) and AI-native V2X systems. We then present a multi-layered threat taxonomy encompassing traditional protocol-level attacks and AI-specific vulnerabilities, including adversarial examples, data poisoning, model inversion, and Byzantine attacks in federated learning environments. Our analysis of defense mechanisms covers machine learning-based intrusion detection systems, blockchain-assisted trust management, federated learning with privacy preservation, and adversarial robustness techniques. We identify critical research gaps, particularly the disconnection between theoretical attack demonstrations and real-world validation, the tension between privacy preservation and detection efficacy, and the unresolved challenge of securing distributed learning under non-IID vehicular data distributions. The review concludes by proposing an integrated security framework that addresses these challenges through explainable AI, adaptive defense mechanisms, and safety-certifiable architectures for next-generation vehicular systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Tools in Neurosurgery: The Indian Perspective: A Narrative Review with PubMed-Based Evidence
items.abstract: Neurosurgery operates in a zone of utmost technical skill and the potential for life-altering outcomes. India faces the added pressure on this specialty from a severe lack of neurosurgeons relative to the nation?s 1.4 billion population. Collectively, neurological diseases contribute to ~6% of the total burden of disease (DALYs) and while the incidence rates of everything from glioblastoma to traumatic brain injury continue to climb, artificial intelligence-comprising machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and natural language processing-has stepped up not as an expensive novel technology but as a leveling influence in this unbalanced environment. Objective: The objective of this narrative review is to survey the spectrum of AI tools presently in use or being vigorously developed in the domain of neurosurgery, with a specific focus on the clinical context in India, institutional endeavors, current evidence, and the practical hurdles in turning promise into regular practice. Methods: A systematic review of the literature on PubMed was performed using combined search terms: artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, neurosurgery, brain tumor, spine surgery, neuro-oncology, India, and robotic surgery. Studies published in peer-reviewed journals from 2017-2024 were emphasized, prioritizing systematic reviews, prospective cohort studies and India-specific institutional reports. Conclusion: AI-powered tools are making contributions to enhance diagnostic accuracy, surgical planning, intraoperative navigation, and postoperative prediction in neurosurgery. India has a demonstrable capacity at the institutional level to drive these advancements, for instance, the AIIMS-IIT Delhi surgical simulator project. However, scalability hinges on future India-specific validation studies, clear regulatory policies, and the balanced investment in robust data infrastructure across public and private healthcare networks.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use and Perceptions Among Three Medical Student Cohorts: Cross-Sectional Comparative Survey Study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly large language models, are increasingly used by medical students, yet patterns of use, perceived reliability, verification practices, and educational expectations may vary across educational contexts. We conducted an exploratory, cross-sectional, anonymous web-based survey at the Albert Szent-Györgyi Medical School, University of Szeged, Hungary, comparing first-year students in the Hungarian-language program (MedHU), first-year students in the English-language program (MedEN), and second- to fifth-year Hungarian-language students enrolled in an AI-focused elective course (MedAI). The author-developed 20-item questionnaire assessed AI use, familiarity, perceived reliability, verification practices, limitations, and educational expectations. Of 550 eligible students, 340 submitted questionnaires and 301 met predefined data-quality criteria. Academic AI use was reported by 81.9% of MedHU, 85.6% of MedEN, and 87.5% of MedAI participants. Use-frequency distributions differed among cohorts (χ2(6) = 64.63, p < 0.001, φ = 0.463); daily use was reported by 43.3% of MedEN, 7.8% of MedHU, and 12.5% of MedAI participants, while familiarity with AI-related terminology varied by term across cohorts. Across cohorts, students generally regarded AI-generated medical information as requiring verification and viewed AI as supplementary to conventional educational resources. These findings identify priorities for AI literacy, particularly critical appraisal, source verification, and responsible use.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Verification and Fault Detection in Digital Logic Circuit Design and Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing complexity of digital logic circuits has made verification and fault detection more difficult, particularly in Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) systems where conventional simulation, Boolean satisfiability (SAT), and automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) methods may require extensive computation. This research examines the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially deep learning, graph-based learning, and ensemble machine learning, as an assistive approach for verifying circuit behavior and detecting faults in combinational and sequential digital circuits. The proposed framework accepts circuit descriptions and test information, extracts structural and behavioral features, applies AI models to classify or predict faults, and returns verification results and diagnostic feedback. Studies on ISCAS benchmark circuits demonstrate that learned models can achieve high fault-classification accuracy and can reduce the search effort associated with traditional techniques. Rather than replacing formal verification, the approach positions AI as a complementary layer that prioritizes suspicious circuit regions, predicts useful test patterns, and accelerates fault analysis. The study concludes that AI-assisted verification can improve scalability and diagnostic efficiency, while formal or simulation-based checks remain necessary to guarantee correctness. Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Digital Logic Circuits, Fault Detection, VLSI Testing, Deep Learning, Automatic Test Pattern Generation, Boolean Satisfiability, Design Verification.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based tongue image analysis for non-invasive screening of gastric cancer, precancerous lesions, and related gastrointestinal disorders: a systematic review
items.abstract: Background Gastric cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, largely because many cases are diagnosed at an advanced stage. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with histopathological confirmation is the diagnostic gold standard, but its invasiveness, cost, and limited accessibility restrict population-level use. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based tongue-image analysis may provide an objective, low-cost, and non-invasive adjunct for pre-endoscopic risk stratification. Methods This systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 principles and was informed by diagnostic test accuracy and prediction-model reporting frameworks. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched from inception to 10 June 2026. Eligible studies were original investigations applying machine-learning or deep-learning methods to digital tongue images for gastric cancer, precancerous gastric lesions, or related gastrointestinal disorders and reporting at least one quantitative performance metric. Data were extracted on study design, sample size, target condition, reference standard, image-acquisition protocol, model architecture, validation strategy, diagnostic performance, calibration, interpretability, and risk of bias. A narrative synthesis was performed because of substantial heterogeneity. Results The search identified 139 records, of which 78 remained after duplicate removal. After title, abstract, and full-text screening, 9 studies published between 2018 and 2025 were included. The evidence covered gastric cancer, precancerous gastric lesions or high-risk gastric screening, and related gastrointestinal disorders. Models included logistic regression and XGBoost classifiers based on handcrafted features, convolutional neural networks, transformer-based architectures, segmentation-assisted pipelines, and multimodal models combining tongue images with clinical, questionnaire, biomarker, or microbiome data. Internally validated AUCs ranged from 0.61 to 0.99 across target conditions. External validation was reported in only three studies and generally showed performance degradation, particularly for precancerous gastric lesions. Calibration assessment was uncommon, and most studies did not report calibration curves, Brier scores, expected calibration error, or recalibration procedures. Conclusion AI-based tongue-image analysis is a promising but early-stage approach for non-invasive gastric disease screening. Current evidence supports its potential role as an adjunctive pre-endoscopic triage tool rather than a replacement for gastroscopy. Prospective external validation, standardized image acquisition, transparent model reporting, calibration assessment, and evaluation in diverse populations are required before clinical deployment. items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Experimental Design and Ethical Considerations: A Case Study of Netflix
items.abstract: The concept of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized scientific research, making it much faster, data-driven, and capable of making decisions. However, its increasing presence in research creates ethical issues regarding the need to balance innovation and responsibility. This paper will discuss how AI-enhanced experimental testing will influence the study methodology through the case study of Netflix. It discusses the importance of platform optimisation, better user interactions, and conversion results using large-scale experimentation to improve the results continuously. Netflix uses AI and machine learning to experiment at the micro level to design the home page, previewing of content, recommendations and pricing in the global user base, resulting in adaptive interfaces and personalised user experiences. Although these practices enhance competitive advantage, they bring up issues of transparency, fairness and user autonomy. This chapter is a critical analysis of how AI-driven experimentation is an indicator of technological innovation and ethical responsibility, and proposes an ethical framework that would cover accountability and sustainable data-driven research in the modern digital world.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Manufacturing and Organisational Effectiveness in the Gambia: The Mediating Role of Human–AI Collaboration and Employee Engagement
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming manufacturing by reshaping production processes, resource allocation, quality management, monitoring, and organisational decision-making. However, the organisational implications of AI adoption cannot be adequately explained from a technological perspective alone. Its effectiveness depends substantially on how employees interact with intelligent technologies and whether organisations create conditions that support adaptation, learning, participation, and engagement. This conceptual article develops an integrated framework explaining the relationship between AI-enabled manufacturing and organisational effectiveness in The Gambia, emphasising human–AI collaboration and employee engagement. Drawing on Kahn’s theory of personal engagement, the Job Demands–Resources model, social exchange theory, self-efficacy theory, and literature on trust in automation and human–AI teaming, the article proposes a sequential mechanism through which AI-enabled manufacturing influences organisational effectiveness through human–AI collaboration and employee engagement. Employee engagement is conceptualised in cognitive and physical/behavioural dimensions, recognising that AI may reduce routine physical effort while increasing cognitive demands associated with monitoring, interpretation, problem-solving, learning, and decision-making. The framework further identifies AI readiness, AI self-efficacy, trust in AI, and organisational support as contextual conditions that may strengthen or weaken these relationships. The Gambia provides a theoretically meaningful context because its emerging manufacturing sector, digital transformation agenda, skills constraints, and need for productive diversification create distinctive conditions for AI adoption. The article contributes an Africa-sensitive conceptual explanation of how technological transformation can generate human and organisational value and provides propositions to guide future empirical research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Diagnosis in the Internet of Medical Things: An End-to-End Survey of Connected Sensing, Distributed Intelligence, Clinical Applications, and Validation
items.abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) can extend diagnostic observation beyond episodic encounters by connecting wearable, point-of-care, imaging, and bedside devices to artificial-intelligence services. Yet continuous measurement is not itself diagnosis: a clinically useful system must establish signal validity, map an output to a defined diagnostic role, communicate uncertainty, and demonstrate agreement with an appropriate reference standard. This survey analyzes the complete IoMT diagnostic pathway from acquisition and quality control through edge–fog–cloud computation, machine and deep learning, federated training, and clinician-governed action. It distinguishes monitoring, screening, early detection, differential diagnosis, prognosis, and decision support because these tasks require different labels, thresholds, metrics, and evidence. Evidence is synthesized across electrocardiography and cardiovascular risk, glucose and metabolic assessment, connected imaging and oncology, respiratory and infectious-disease detection, electroencephalography and seizure recognition, and decentralized point-of-care testing. The analysis shows how sensor placement, missingness, compression, latency, privacy mechanisms, and site heterogeneity can change diagnostic performance even when the model is unchanged. A diagnostic evidence framework is therefore proposed that links reference standards and patient-level data separation to sensitivity, specificity, calibration, external validation, target-device feasibility, uncertainty-based referral, and prospective workflow utility. Security, explainability, and lifecycle monitoring are treated as conditions of diagnostic reliability rather than independent features. The resulting synthesis provides a clinically centered basis for deciding which IoMT outputs may support screening or diagnosis, which remain monitoring signals, and what evidence is still required before deployment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, augmented reality, and virtual reality in science education: scientific mapping and future research
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the trends, thematic development, and research collaboration patterns related to Artificial Intelligence (AI), Augmented Reality (AR), and Virtual Reality (VR) in science education through a comprehensive bibliometric analysis. The rapid integration of these emerging technologies has increased the demand for innovative learning approaches capable of enhancing student engagement, conceptual understanding, and immersive learning experiences in science education. Bibliometric analysis was conducted using Scopus-indexed publications from 2014 to 2024, comprising 196 articles. Data were analyzed using VOSviewer, Microsoft Excel, and the Biblioshiny package in R program to identify publication trends, citation patterns, author collaborations, and thematic research developments. The findings reveal a substantial increase in research productivity related to AI, AR, and VR in science education, with the United States and Turkey emerging as dominant contributors. The analysis also indicates growing research interest in immersive learning, adaptive instruction, and interdisciplinary integration. Highly cited studies demonstrate the potential of these technologies to improve student engagement, academic performance, and knowledge retention. However, challenges related to technological accessibility, scalability, physical discomfort, and long-term implementation remain insufficiently explored. This study provides important insights into the evolving landscape of AI, AR, and VR research in science education and highlights the need for more sustainable, inclusive, and context-sensitive approaches to technology integration in future educational research and practice.

items.title: ASAS-NANP SYMPOSIUM: MATHEMATICAL MODELING IN ANIMAL NUTRITION: Data-efficient Computer Vision for Precision Livestock Farming
items.abstract: Abstract Precision livestock farming (PLF) increasingly relies on computer vision (CV) to monitor animal behavior, health, and production. However, widespread adoption remains limited by the large quantities of manually labeled data required to train most artificial intelligence (AI) models. This paper reviews AI and CV applications in PLF and presents three data-efficient case studies conducted at a research feedlot at Texas A&M University. The assessment of AI model predictability was conducted with precision, recall, F1-score, and adjusted rand index (ARI). In Case Study 1, a data-efficient Mask R-CNN model pre-trained on the COCO dataset was applied without modification to detect cattle feeding events at individual feed bunks. Across 98,720 frame-bunk classifications, the system achieved 87.2% precision, 89.1% recall, and an 88.2% F1 score compared to physical bunk sensor ground truth. In Case Study 2, transfer learning on a ResNet backbone was used to classify bunk feed grade across six customized levels (S00–S40) using only 183 labelled images. The model achieved 91% accuracy on an independent verification set of 7,905 images. In Case Study 3, statistical tools, i.e., Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) and k-means clustering, were applied to identify individual animals at the bunk without manual animal-level annotation. This method and achieved an ARI of 0.96 against expert-verified ground truth, successfully differentiating animals. Integrating all three components, the framework produced a continuous record of individual animal bunk visits and estimated feed intake from a one-hour video. Key remaining challenges include long-term individual animal re-identification under changing appearance and environmental conditions, incorporation of spatiotemporal information to better characterize feeding behavior, and the limited availability of large-scale open datasets for PLF research. Future research will integrate multispectral imaging and audio analytics to improve model robustness and advance individual animal identification for cattle health and nutritional management.

items.title: Assessing Individual Differences in Adult Theory of Mind Through Mental State Language: Human and Artificial Intelligence Approaches
items.abstract: Theory of mind is central to human social behavior, yet empirical studies rely largely on biased measures with limited ecological validity. We propose and evaluate the use of mental state language as a spontaneous indicator of theory of mind expressed in social interaction. Among research participants (334 undergraduate students, 63.8% non-Hispanic White, 74.3% female) engaged in a dyadic cooperative task with an unfamiliar peer, mental state language demonstrated strong convergent validity with established measures of theory of mind and, when compared to established measures, superior predictive validity for interpersonal functioning. Fine-tuned transformers and open-source generative large language models reliably replicated human coding of mental state language, enabling scalable assessment. These findings offer promising initial construct-validity evidence for mental state language as a measure of theory of mind, and motivate its extension to naturalistic, dynamically unfolding social interactions.

items.title: Assessment Instruments for Generative AI Literacy in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Measurement Approaches, Psychometric Properties, and Implications for SDG 4
items.abstract: Assessment of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) literacy in higher education draws on both GenAI-specific instruments and broader artificial intelligence (AI) literacy measures, but these evidence sources are not interchangeable. This systematic review examined the GenAI-literacy assessment landscape while distinguishing direct GenAI-specific evidence from general AI-literacy evidence. Following PRISMA 2020 and a registered INPLASY protocol, four electronic information sources were searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies published from 2022 through 26 July 2026. Thirty-one studies met the eligibility criteria: 23 (74.2%) assessed general AI literacy, whereas eight (25.8%) used GenAI-specific instruments. Self-report Likert-type scales predominated (n = 28; 90.3%); performance-based and hybrid approaches were uncommon. Psychometric evidence centered on internal consistency and factor structure, while temporal stability, measurement invariance, external validity, and item-level functioning were rarely examined. Potential implications were mapped to digital competencies, quality education, and responsible AI use, but inclusive learning appeared in only 11 studies (35.5%). Conclusions about GenAI-specific assessment are therefore limited to eight studies. The evidence indicates a need for GenAI-specific hybrid instruments, broader validation, and accessible performance tasks. Such assessment can inform education but constitutes a diagnostic contribution to SDG 4 rather than evidence of its achievement.

items.title: Assessment profiles in undergraduate dental anatomy education: a five-year retrospective analysis with implications for future AI-supported question Bank Development
items.abstract: Longitudinal examination data can provide valuable evidence for monitoring assessment quality in health professions education. In dental anatomy education, such evidence is particularly relevant because assessment should support both foundational anatomical knowledge and later clinical application. The growing interest in artificial intelligence-supported item generation further increases the need to understand existing local assessment profiles before developing AI-assisted question banks. Archived individual-level final examination records from first- and second-year undergraduate dental anatomy courses were retrospectively analysed across five academic years, from 2021–2022 to 2025–2026. Final examination scores were evaluated as continuous variables and categorised into predefined achievement bands. Class-level differences, year-to-year variation and achievement band distributions were examined using non-parametric and categorical statistical analyses. AI-generated questions were not administered to students and did not contribute to grades. A total of 1,216 eligible final examination records were analysed, comprising 666 first-year and 550 s-year records. The overall mean final examination score was 63.91 ± 20.00, with a median score of 66.0. Final examination scores differed significantly across academic years ( p < 0.001). Although second-year scores were numerically higher overall, the class-level difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.072). Five-year final examination data demonstrated meaningful longitudinal variation in undergraduate dental anatomy assessment performance. The elevated 2021–2022 performance coincided with pandemic-era online assessment conditions; however, the available data do not permit causal attribution of the higher scores to the online examination format. The findings provide a local retrospective assessment baseline that may inform future AI-assisted question bank development, while also indicating the need for expert review and prospective item-level psychometric validation before AI-assisted items are used in student assessment.

items.title: Attentional allocation in simulated aerial engagement: an ERP and eye-tracking study
items.abstract: Aerial engagement is critical for seising air superiority and operations outcomes, yet pilots’ attentional allocation in such tasks remains poorly understood. This study used ERP and eye-tracking measures to investigate attentional allocation in 44 pilots during 1v1 simulated aerial engagements. ERP data were analysed using spatiotemporal cluster-based permutation tests; eye-tracking measures were compared using one-way ANOVA. An event-wise significant winner–loser ERP difference was found following the Enemy Tracking event, characterised by a right frontal P3a in winners, with losers showing the opposite polarity (161–317 ms, p = 0.046). Winners also exhibited smaller pupil diameter, higher fixation proportion, and higher AOI hit rate. These findings suggest the Enemy Tracking event is a critical attentional window, where attentional allocation and behavioural responses – reflected in distinct right frontal processing modes – are closely associated with engagement outcomes. This may inform targeted training interventions and neuroergonomic assessment tools to enhance attentional efficiency.

items.title: Automation-Induced Redundancy: Does Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act Provide Adequate Safeguards in the Era of Generative AI?
items.abstract: Abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence, especially Generative AI, is really changing how we work and what employment looks like. While these AI technologies can boost productivity and enhance decision-making, they might also lessen the need for human workers in some roles, leading to layoffs and job losses. This shift has sparked worries about job security, potential layoffs, the need for reskilling, and whether current labor laws are adequate. This research examines whether the safeguards provide under Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act from 1947 are enough to protect employees whose jobs are impacted by automation and tech advancements. It zooms in on key legal protections related to layoffs, notice periods, compensation, required government approvals, and other employee safeguards. Additionally, it looks at the challenges posed by Generative AI, especially how tech changes can shift job roles, cut down the demand for certain skills, or even render some positions obsolete. The study takes a doctrinal and qualitative approach, pulling from a variety of sources like legislation, court rulings, academic research, government documents, and insights into AI, automation, and employment. It also examines the Industrial Relations Code of 2020 to grasp how India's labor law framework is evolving in light of technology. The findings indicate that while current labor laws do offer crucial protections during layoffs, they might not fully tackle the issues brought on by AI-related job changes. There's a strong suggestion that more focus is needed on reskilling, redeploying, transparency, and providing support during transitions before any layoffs occur. Therefore, the study advocates for a more employee-centered approach, encouraging employers to prioritize reskilling and redeployment ahead of layoffs, while also balancing tech advancements, business demands, and employee rights. items.title: Autonomous Scientific Discovery via Exploration Schema Libraries: Replicating Scientists' Problem-Space Metacognition
items.abstract: Current Artificial Intelligence for Science (AI4S) frameworks excel at pattern recognition within massive datasets but fundamentally lack causal reasoning and the capacity for autonomous theoretical innovation. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel paradigm that shifts the focus from learning scientific data to learning the metacognitive exploration behaviors of historical scientists. We propose modeling a scientist's cognitive journey—such as proposing heuristic conjectures, navigating complex problem spaces, and inventing paradigm-shifting representational tools (e.g., Feynman diagrams)—into a formalized, reusable "Exploration Schema Library". By designing a dual-loop mechanism powered by Inverse Reinforcement Learning, AI can harvest these high-level strategic patterns from scientific history and structurally project them onto modern unresolved theoretical frameworks. This approach offers a distinct, cognitively grounded pathway toward achieving autonomous causal discovery in next-generation artificial intelligence.
